problem_markdown: Fix distinct plane points $O,A$. For $X\ne O$, let $\alpha(X)\in[0,2\pi)$ be the counterclockwise angle from $OA$ to $OX$, and let $C(X)$ have centre $O$ and radius $OX+\alpha(X)/OX$. Prove that every finite colouring of the plane has a point $Y$ with $\alpha(Y)>0$ whose colour occurs on $C(Y)$.
solutions_markdown:
Suppose there are $k$ colours. For each radius $r\in[1,2]$, record the nonempty set of colours appearing on the circle centred at $O$ of radius $r$. There are at most $2^k$ such sets, so among $2^k+1$ distinct radii two, say $r<R$, have the same colour set.

Choose $Y$ at radius $r$ and angle $\theta=r(R-r)$. This angle is strictly positive and less than two, hence less than $2\pi$. By definition, $C(Y)$ has radius $r+\theta/r=R$. The colour of $Y$ appears on the smaller circle and therefore on the larger circle because their colour sets are identical. This is exactly the desired conclusion.
